clinicalPearls: Presents with sudden severe pain, foreign body sensation, tearing, photophobia, and blepharospasm, usually after minor trauma such as a fingernail, branch, or contact lens
Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals the epithelial defect as a bright green area
Always evert the upper lid and inspect for a retained subtarsal foreign body, especially with vertical linear (ice-rink) abrasions
Topical anaesthetic aids examination but must never be prescribed for ongoing use as it delays healing and masks damage
Small uncomplicated abrasions heal within one to two days; treatment is supportive with lubrication and topical antibiotic prophylaxis
Contact lens-related abrasions and those from vegetable or organic matter carry higher infection risk and warrant closer follow-up
Patching is generally avoided, particularly in contact lens wearers, as it may promote infection
reference.pathophysiology: A corneal abrasion is a defect in the corneal epithelium, most often from mechanical trauma. Loss of the epithelial barrier exposes richly innervated subepithelial nerve endings, producing intense pain and reflex tearing and blepharospasm. The epithelium normally regenerates rapidly by sliding and mitosis of surrounding cells. Contamination, retained foreign material, or contact lens wear can convert a simple abrasion into a microbial keratitis, and repeated or poorly healing defects may reflect an underlying epithelial basement membrane dystrophy causing recurrent erosions.
additionalDifferentials: Retained corneal or subtarsal foreign body
additionalInvestigations: Fluorescein staining to delineate the epithelial defect
Upper lid eversion to exclude a retained subtarsal foreign body
Slit-lamp examination to assess depth and look for infiltrate suggesting infection
Contact lens history and, if infiltrate present, corneal scrape for microbiology
redFlags: A white corneal infiltrate, mucopurulent discharge, or anterior chamber reaction suggesting microbial keratitis
Contact lens wearers with pain out of proportion, indicating possible Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba infection
Failure to heal within expected time or worsening pain and redness
Suspicion of penetrating injury or high-velocity foreign body
reference.prognosis: Simple abrasions heal quickly with no lasting visual effect, but infection, deep central lesions, or recurrent erosions can cause scarring and reduced vision.
pitfalls: Sending patients home with topical anaesthetic, which delays healing and can cause severe corneal damage
Failing to evert the lid and missing a retained foreign body
Patching a contact lens wearer and precipitating infection
Assuming all painful epithelial defects are simple abrasions and missing herpetic or microbial keratitis
management: Prescribe topical antibiotic prophylaxis, using an agent with anti-pseudomonal cover such as a fluoroquinolone for contact lens-related abrasions
Provide analgesia with oral analgesics and a topical cycloplegic to ease ciliary spasm and photophobia, supplemented by ocular lubricants
Remove any foreign body and always evert the upper lid to exclude a retained subtarsal foreign body
Never prescribe topical anaesthetics for ongoing use as they delay healing and mask damage, and avoid patching contact lens-related abrasions
Advise cessation of contact lens wear until the epithelium has fully healed
Arrange follow-up and refer to ophthalmology for non-healing defects, a stromal infiltrate suggesting microbial keratitis, or organic-matter injury
Manage recurrent erosions with prolonged lubrication and hypertonic saline ointment
